To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
higher caregiver perceived economic hardship and psychological distress and higher disease activity were associated with worse HRQOL in children with JIA.

caregiver perceived economic hardship is a significant predictor of children’s HRQoL, and caregiver psychological distress and higher disease activity in children are also significant predictors of children’s HRQL.
caregiver financial hardship, psychological distress and children’s disease activity are associated with worse health-related quality of living in children with JIA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how children’s disease activity impacts children’s HRQoL.
the impact of economic and social disadvantage on health outcomes of children and adolescents with JIA.
the impact of economic hardship on health-related quality of live in children with juvenile arthritis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the study results suggest that the association between economic hardship and psychological distress on the one hand and children’s HRQL on the other is mediated through the disease activity.
caregiver perceived financial hardship, psychological distress and children’s disease activity are associated with worse children with JIA’s health outcomes.
caregiver financial hardship is associated with poorer HRQOL in children with JIA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
economic hardships and psychological distress of caregivers are associated with children’s disease activity and HRQOL.
the more economic hardship and the more disease activity the child has, the more the parent will be psychologically distressed and the child will have worse quality of life.
economic hardship, caregiver distress and disease activity all have an impact on the HRQoL of children with JIA.
The main takeaway from our work is that

children with JIA are a particularly vulnerable group and that health professionals need to be vigilant in assessing the psychosocial and financial situation of these families and in providing them with the appropriate supports.
children’s HRQoL is not only influenced by disease activity, but it is also impacted by the family’s financial situation and caregiver psychological well-being.
health providers should consider the economic and psychosocial factors of the family when assessing children with JIA and when planning treatment.
